hints: Notice the question asks for the meaning of e.m.f. of $6 \text{ V}$, which has units $\text{J C}^{-1}$, not just a voltage across a resistor.
Recall the governing relation $E = W/Q$, where $W$ is the chemical energy transformed inside the cell and $Q$ is the charge passing through it.
Compare total energy supplied per coulomb with energy lost in internal resistance and energy delivered to the external circuit to see which statement matches $6 \text{ J}$ per $1 \text{ C}$.
walkthrough: Identify the given information: the cell has e.m.f. $E = 6 \text{ V}$, meaning $6$ joules per coulomb in SI base terms.
State the physical rule: e.m.f. is defined as $E = W/Q$, the chemical potential energy transformed to electrical energy inside the source per unit charge passing through it.
Apply to $Q = 1 \text{ C}$: $W = E Q = 6 \text{ V} \times 1 \text{ C} = 6 \text{ J}$ of chemical energy transformed.
Check the distractors: internal resistance accounts for only part of $W$, one electron carries only $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, and terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$ is less than $E$ when $I > 0$.
Therefore $1 \text{ C}$ through the cell corresponds to $6 \text{ J}$ transformed. This is option D.

options.A: This describes only energy lost in internal resistance, not total energy supplied by the cell per coulomb.
options.B: E.m.f. is energy per coulomb, not per electron; 1 electron has charge $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ so gains much less than $6 \text{ J}$.
options.C: Terminal p.d. across an external circuit is less than $6 \text{ V}$ when current flows because some e.m.f. is lost across internal resistance.
options.D: E.m.f. is chemical energy transformed to electrical energy per unit charge, so $6 \text{ V}$ means $6 \text{ J}$ per $1 \text{ C}$.
